Defects: score_fresh docstring says 'independent draws' but the cyclic pairing makes adjacent penalty terms dependent (model.py:101-106); star imports in __init__, run.py and tests; test class named T; run.py:71-72 calls table_stats three times and recomputes the asymptotic SD inline instead of via plugin_stats; phi_inv by 80-step bisection where statistics.NormalDist.inv_cdf exists. A reviewer would accept after the score_fresh fix.
evidence.claims: Backed by results.txt and reproduced: 0.0199 vs 0.208 rent, 0.028 fresh, tau 0.045/0.083/0.113, 40% honest-pay cost (1-0.1253/0.2079=39.7%), 22-54% for 75-99% rent removal, n=329/115/56 and 870/242/72, 'exact variance verified by enumeration', 'constant reporter paid exactly 0' (tested). Not backed or overstated: README:3 gives the variance formula of the unbiased sample covariance as the payment's variance, without the (2(n-1)/n)^2 factor the whitepaper carries; whitepaper:6 says 'exact finite-sample law' but only the first two moments are exact (the rent uses a normal approximation); abstract 'sqrt 2 exactly at the null' holds only when both marginals are 1/2 (at p=0.2, peer a=b=0.9 the null SD ratio is 1.61); README 'hit 95% in simulation' and whitepaper 'reach 95%' vs 0.941/0.944 simulated and 0.938 exact; '1.39-1.64x noisier' (E2) uses the independent-pair formula, which the simulated scheme departs from at p=0.2. No prior work is cited at all; Dasgupta-Ghosh is named without a reference.
evidence.fitness: A researcher could pick up the moment formulas and the joint-table code and extend them. For a paper, the nearest prior work is uncited: Dasgupta & Ghosh 2013 (WWW) and Shnayder et al. 2016 (EC, correlated agreement) for the mechanism; Agarwal et al. (peer prediction with heterogeneous users, sample complexity) and Kong's DMI mechanism (constant number of tasks) for finite-task analysis; Witkowski et al. 2013 ('Dwelling on the negative', limited liability and effort) and Gao, Wright & Leyton-Brown 2016 for effort incentives and noise. The variance of a sample covariance is textbook, and E[S+]=sigma/sqrt(2 pi) is the folded-normal mean, so the novel part is the framing (noise rent and deductible sizing), which is a workshop-note contribution, not a main-track result. Not listed as a programme step in research/PROGRAMMES.md.
evidence.domain: Sound as statistics: exact moments, normal tail for rent, a standard one-sided z-test sample size (power slightly under target at small n, as expected from the normal approximation). As mechanism design it departs from practice in three places a reviewer would hit: (1) the 'fresh' baseline is a constructed variant drawing a second sample of n tasks with independent-looking penalty pairs, not the Dasgupta-Ghosh mechanism, which takes penalty tasks from the same batch, so the sqrt 2 saving is against a strawman that also uses twice the tasks; (2) no incentive analysis of the floored plug-in payment (is truthful reporting still a best response under max(S,0) and a deductible, and what about lazy strategies other than a fair coin, e.g. q-coins chosen against the deductible); (3) p and peer quality are assumed known when sizing n and tau, with no sensitivity analysis.

defects.what: Fresh-penalty simulator does not implement the scheme its variance formula describes: score_fresh pairs u_k with v_(k+1) cyclically in one second sample, so adjacent penalty terms share a task and covary by (2f_i-1)(2f_j-1)Cov; off f_i=1/2 the simulated variance exceeds (a(1-a)+pi(1-pi))/n (2.162e-3 vs 1.922e-3 at p=0.2, g=0.8, n=200). E2's p=0.2 ratios (1.39-1.50) describe the formula, not the code; every validation sits at f_i=0.5 where the error vanishes.

No prior work cited and novelty overstated: the variance of a sample covariance is textbook and E[S+]=sigma/sqrt(2 pi) is the folded-normal mean; Dasgupta & Ghosh 2013, Shnayder et al. 2016 (correlated agreement), Kong's DMI mechanism, Agarwal et al. (sample complexity, heterogeneous users), Witkowski et al. 2013 (limited liability and effort) are not referenced.

Baseline is a constructed 'fresh' scheme that draws a second sample of n tasks (2n total), not the Dasgupta-Ghosh mechanism, which draws penalty tasks from the same batch; the sqrt 2 / 1.39-1.64x saving is measured against it.

sample_size (behind every E4 number and the figure) is untested in effect: using sd0 for the power term or a two-sided alpha (n +20%: 329/115/56 -> 396/139/68) leaves all tests green; no test pins results.txt.
README states the unbiased-sample-covariance variance as the plug-in payment's exact variance, omitting the (2(n-1)/n)^2 factor the whitepaper carries.
'Exact finite-sample law' claims more than the exact first two moments given; 'sqrt 2 exactly at the null' holds only when both marginals are 1/2 (1.61 at p=0.2, peer a=b=0.9).
'Hit/reach 95% in simulation' for detection: simulated 0.950/0.944/0.941, exact 0.9485/0.9449/0.9380; the normal-approximation n undershoots at small n and the text does not say so.
No incentive analysis of the floored/deductible payment: only a fair coin and a constant are tried as lazy strategies, and truthful best response under max(S - tau, 0) is not checked.

verdict: Every headline number reproduces: run.py output is byte-identical to results.txt, and an independent exact multinomial enumeration matches the plug-in variance (0.057600/0.040918/0.029747/0.009904/0.002045), the lazy-coin rent (0.01985 exact vs 0.0199) and the deductible table (tau 0.0448/0.0826/0.1128, honest pay 0.1631/0.1254/0.0955). The gap is elsewhere. The fresh-penalty simulator pairs tasks cyclically, so its variance departs from the formula E2 reports once marginals leave 1/2 (12% in variance at p=0.2, g=0.8), and the baseline is a constructed scheme using twice the tasks rather than Dasgupta-Ghosh as published. Two of five seeded mutants in sample_size survive (a +20% change in every E4 n). The README's variance formula drops the (2(n-1)/n)^2 factor, '95%' is 93.8-94.9%, and no prior work is cited for what is mostly textbook statistics with a new framing. Correct and well-built as a note; not at the bar for claims, verification or a peer-prediction reviewer.
